subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that the points (1,1), (−6,0), (−2,2) and (−2,−8) are concyclic.

mark_split.label: Radius and the equation of the circle
Show D lies on the circle

insider_note: Concyclic means one circle through all four, so build the circle from any three and then test the fourth — that last substitution is a printed mark of its own and is the line students most often leave out.

steps.label: First equation from SA = SB
steps.margin_note: First printed mark, tagged "1 Mark" in the book beside equation (1).
steps.memory_tip: Four points, but only three are used to build the circle. Keep D back as the test.
lines: Let S(x₁, y₁) be the centre of the circle
through A, B and C ⇒ SA = SB = SC
steps.why: Four points are concyclic when one circle passes through all of them. Three points fix a circle, so the circle is built from A, B and C and the fourth point is checked afterwards.
common_mistakes: Trying to force all four points into the distance conditions at once.
Losing the y₁² term of B because B has y = 0.

steps.label: Second equation from SB = SC
steps.margin_note: Second printed mark, tagged "1 Mark" beside equation (2). The book pairs B with C here, not A with C.
steps.memory_tip: Any two of the three equalities work. B and C are chosen because B has a zero coordinate.
steps.why: Any two of the three equal-distance conditions are enough; the third follows. Pairing B with C keeps the numbers small because B has y = 0.
common_mistakes: Dividing 8x₁ + 4y₁ + 28 = 0 by 4 and writing the constant as 4.

steps.label: Solve for the centre
steps.margin_note: Two printed marks, tagged "2 Marks" beside the centre. Both equations have coefficient 1 on y₁, so subtract.
steps.memory_tip: Both equations end in y₁, so subtracting removes y₁ in one line.
steps.why: The two perpendicular bisectors meet at the centre. Because y₁ has coefficient 1 in both, one subtraction gives x₁ directly.
common_mistakes: Substituting x₁ = −2 as 7(2) and getting y₁ = −31.

steps.label: Radius and the equation of the circle
steps.margin_note: Two printed marks, tagged "2 Marks". Radius and equation are one block in the book, so keep them together.
steps.memory_tip: r² = 25 is a perfect square, which is a quick sign that the arithmetic so far is right.
lines: A = (1, 1) lies on the circle, so r = SA.
Circle with centre (−2, −3) and r² = 25 is
steps.why: This is the circle through A, B and C. Its equation has to be written out in general form because the fourth point is about to be substituted into it.
common_mistakes: Stopping at (x + 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25, which makes the next substitution slower.
Getting the constant as +12 instead of −12.

steps.label: Show D lies on the circle
steps.margin_note: The last printed mark, tagged "1 Mark". Substitute and show the value is exactly 0, then write the conclusion sentence.
steps.memory_tip: Substituting a point into the left side gives 0 only when the point is on the circle.

lines.text: ∴ The four given points are concyclic.

steps.why: A point lies on a circle exactly when substituting its coordinates into the left side of the general equation gives 0. Since the circle already passes through A, B and C, showing D also satisfies it proves all four lie on one circle.
common_mistakes: Getting a non-zero value from a sign slip and then claiming the points are concyclic anyway.
Leaving out the final sentence, which carries the conclusion mark.
